alternatives: Insulin in place of metformin while the cirrhosis is decompensated.
For hypertension, if it persists off diuretics, an agent other than an ACE inhibitor or angiotensin receptor blocker.
contraindications: Lisinopril: ACE inhibitors are not recommended in cirrhosis with ascites (hypotension, kidney injury).
interactions: Furosemide 80 mg with spironolactone 100 mg: the loop diuretic now exceeds the usual 100:40 ratio; loop escalation causes hypokalemia and metabolic alkalosis, both of which increase renal ammoniagenesis.
Furosemide and spironolactone in overt hepatic encephalopathy with potassium 2.9 mEq/L: hold until the encephalopathy and potassium have resolved, then restart at a 100:40 ratio with monitoring.
Metformin in decompensated cirrhosis (bilirubin 3.2 mg/dL, INR 1.7) with creatinine 1.3 mg/dL: risk of lactic acidosis; hold.
Atorvastatin 40 mg in decompensated cirrhosis: use a lower dose with monitoring for muscle and liver toxicity.
Lactulose and rifaximin: no clinically relevant interaction with the current medicines.

prohibited_recommendations: Do not give benzodiazepines or other sedatives for agitation or sleep: they precipitate and prolong hepatic encephalopathy; manage agitation with reorientation, a safe environment and treatment of the precipitant (EASL 2022).
Do not prescribe opioids, which worsen HE; for pain use acetaminophen up to 2 g per day.
Do not escalate the loop diuretic while potassium is low; the diuretic regimen needs potassium and creatinine monitoring.
required_recommendations: Identify and treat the precipitants: the furosemide increase (potassium 2.9 mEq/L with metabolic alkalosis) and the missed lactulose with two days of constipation.

Replace potassium to 4.0 mEq/L or more, because hypokalemia increases renal ammoniagenesis, and replace magnesium (1.6 mg/dL); hold furosemide and spironolactone while overt HE and hypokalemia persist (EASL 2018).

Give parenteral thiamine before any dextrose: bariatric surgery and a week of nausea with poor intake put her at risk of thiamine deficiency; if ophthalmoplegia, nystagmus or ataxia appears, treat as Wernicke encephalopathy with thiamine 200 mg IV three times daily (EFNS 2010).

Once HE and potassium have resolved, restart the diuretics at the 100:40 spironolactone-to-furosemide ratio with potassium and creatinine monitoring, and treat symptomatic ascites with large-volume paracentesis and albumin rather than loop-diuretic escalation (EASL 2018).

Lactulose 25 mL every 1-2 hours until at least two soft bowel movements, then titrated to 2-3 soft bowel movements per day (ACG 2026 recommendation 10; EASL 2022); avoid over-titration, which causes dehydration, hypokalemia and kidney injury.
Continue rifaximin 550 mg twice daily with lactulose for this recurrent overt episode (ACG 2026; EASL 2022).

Stop metformin (decompensated cirrhosis, lactic acidosis risk) and manage glucose with insulin; stop lisinopril (ACE inhibitors are not recommended with ascites; EASL 2018); lower the atorvastatin dose with monitoring (Baveno VII).
Educate the patient and her daughter: lactulose is titrated to 2-3 soft stools a day and not stopped, and diuretic doses are not changed without a potassium and creatinine check.
Refer for liver transplant assessment: decompensated cirrhosis with recurrent overt HE, MELD-Na 21 (EASL 2018).

avoided_actions.rationale: No clinical suspicion for hepatopulmonary syndrome, portopulmonary hypertension, or endocarditis; echocardiography is not part of the HE workup.
Amyloid PET has no role in HE workup; reversible metabolic encephalopathy is the issue, not Alzheimer pathology.
DaTscan has no role in HE workup; the question is metabolic encephalopathy, not nigrostriatal degeneration.
Early-onset AD genetic panel has no role in HE workup; reversible metabolic encephalopathy is the diagnosis under consideration.
Visual evoked potentials have no role in HE workup; no demyelinating process is on the differential.

accepted: Hepatic encephalopathy (West Haven grade II), NASH cirrhosis (Child-Pugh C, MELD-Na 21), precipitated by iatrogenic hypokalemia from excessive furosemide and lactulose non-adherence

differential.key_features: Bariatric surgery 3 years ago and a week of nausea with poor intake raise the risk; extraocular movements are intact, and the confusion is explained by the hypokalemia and missed lactulose. Not excluded clinically; thiamine is given empirically.
Excluded: ascitic PMN 95 cells/mm3, Gram stain negative, culture no growth.
Diabetes, hypertension and obesity raise the risk, but there is no focal deficit; dysarthria and asterixis are global, and CT if obtained shows no infarct.

key_clinical_evidence: Child-Pugh C (13: bilirubin 3.2 3, albumin 2.7 3, INR 1.7 2, moderate ascites 3, HE grade 2 2); MELD-Na 21 (creatinine 1.3, bilirubin 3.2, INR 1.7, sodium 134)
HE is a clinical diagnosis: West Haven grading, evidence of liver dysfunction and exclusion of other causes of altered mental status (ACG 2026; EASL 2022).

An elevated ammonia neither grades nor confirms hepatic encephalopathy and repeat levels are not used to guide treatment; a normal ammonia in a confused patient with cirrhosis should prompt a search for another cause (ACG 2026 recommendation 5 and key concept 14; EASL 2022).

Precipitant identification is more actionable than the ammonia number: infection (SBP especially), GI bleeding, electrolyte disturbance (hypokalemia, hyponatremia), constipation, sedatives, dehydration and kidney injury (ACG 2026; EASL 2022).
Hypokalemia and metabolic alkalosis increase renal ammoniagenesis and the diffusion of ammonia into the brain; the 100:40 spironolactone-to-furosemide ratio helps keep potassium balanced (EASL 2018).
Lactulose non-adherence is one of the most common modifiable HE precipitants: counsel titration to stools and not stopping when feeling well.

patient.history_present_illness: A 52-year-old woman with known NASH cirrhosis was brought to the emergency department by her daughter after two days of worsening confusion and slurred speech. Her daughter reports that the patient had been complaining of increased abdominal distension and had called her primary care provider about it three days ago. She had been told to increase her furosemide dose from 40 mg to 80 mg per day on her own, which she did. Over the following two days, she became progressively more confused, sleeping most of the day, mixing up names of grandchildren, and leaving the stove on twice. On the morning of admission, she called her daughter by the wrong name and did not recognize her son-in-law. She denied headache, fever, vision changes, or weakness. She denied chest pain or shortness of breath. She had been compliant with lactulose and rifaximin until two days ago when her daughter noticed she had forgotten multiple doses of lactulose. Her last bowel movement was two days ago. She had no recent travel, sick contacts, or dietary changes. She had been eating less than usual over the past week due to nausea. She has no history of seizures and drinks alcohol only rarely. Her prior hepatic encephalopathy episode six months ago had resolved with lactulose optimization over 48 hours. On review of her recent labs from one week prior, her potassium was borderline low at 3.4 mEq/L, and her creatinine was at her baseline of 1.0 mg/dL. Her family denies any falls, head trauma, or new medications.
